topicName: Operating System Level Tuning (IO, NUMA, Swapping)
content: [{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"Operating System Level Tuning for MySQL: IO, NUMA, and Swapping"},{"order":2,"type":"paragraph","text":"Achieving peak performance for MySQL workloads requires extending optimization beyond the database configuration file and into the underlying operating system. Proper tuning of Input/Output (IO) subsystems, Non-Uniform Memory Access (NUMA) nodes, and memory swapping behaviors can drastically improve throughput and reduce query latency."},{"order":3,"type":"subheading","text":"1. I/O Subsystem Optimization"},{"order":4,"type":"paragraph","text":"Database performance is frequently bound by disk I/O. Choosing the correct storage scheduler and configuring mount options can eliminate bottlenecks associated with random reads and writes common in transactional workloads."},{"order":5,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Disk Scheduler: For fast NVMe or SSD drives, use the none or kyber scheduler to reduce CPU overhead. For traditional rotational HDDs, use bfq or deadline."},{"order":6,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Mount Options: Mount data volumes with the noatime option to prevent unnecessary disk writes on file read operations."},{"order":7,"type":"code","text":"echo none > /sys/block/nvme0n1/queue/scheduler"},{"order":8,"type":"subheading","text":"2. NUMA (Non-Uniform Memory Access) Tuning"},{"order":9,"type":"paragraph","text":"Modern multi-socket servers use NUMA architecture, where CPU sockets have localized memory banks. When a CPU accesses memory on another socket, latency increases. MySQL can suffer from unpredictable performance degradation due to remote memory access."},{"order":10,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Check NUMA topology using the numactl --hardware command."},{"order":11,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Configure interleave memory policies or bind mysqld to a single NUMA node if the database fits entirely within that node's memory."},{"order":12,"type":"code","text":"numactl --interleave=all mysqld"},{"order":13,"type":"subheading","text":"3. Swapping and Memory Management"},{"order":14,"type":"paragraph","text":"Swapping database pages to disk causes catastrophic drops in MySQL performance. The Linux kernel's swappiness parameter controls how aggressively anonymous memory pages are swapped out."},{"order":15,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Set vm.swappiness to a low value (e.g., 1) to discourage the kernel from swapping database memory."},{"order":16,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Configure vm.overcommit_memory to ensure memory allocation behaves predictably under heavy loads."},{"order":17,"type":"code","text":"sysctl -w vm.swappiness=1"},{"order":18,"type":"heading","text":"Conclusion"},{"order":19,"type":"paragraph","text":"By aligning your Linux kernel parameters with MySQL requirements—specifically optimizing disk schedulers, handling NUMA correctly, and minimizing swapping—you establish a robust foundation for high-availability database deployments."}]
